subject: research/qual-lowrate
professional: a survey statistician or biostatistician who designs two-phase / stratified validation samples (Cochran-style optimum allocation, Horvitz-Thompson weighting, misclassification-corrected prevalence). They would check first that the estimator is the textbook stratified one, that coverage is simulated against a known truth, and that the Wald interval is not trusted at tiny stratum counts; then whether the finding (optimum allocation to the noisy stratum is high, not low) is new.

evidence.correctness: Ran `cd research/qual-lowrate && python3 experiments/run.py` (8.7 s wall, cache already present): output diffed against the committed results.txt, no difference at all (git status clean). Then wrote scratchpad indep.py, which does not import qualrate/qualaudit: its own csv loader (reusing only the NEGATIVE and LEXICON data sets from qual-real), own stratified estimator and Wald SE in numpy, own Monte Carlo (4,000 draws, numpy Generator). Recomputed: (1) corpus n=5313, evaluated 3188, truth 0.24686 (README 0.2469): match. (2) Lexicon coder: coded-positive 0.1484, precision 0.617, recall 0.371, miss rate 0.1553, Neyman negative share 0.820 (results.txt 0.148, 0.617, 0.371, 0.1553, 0.820): exact. (3) Lexicon, 200 items, 50% negatives: coverage 0.953 / width 0.1315 (results 0.958 / 0.131); 100 items at 2%: coverage 0.302 / width 0.525 (results 0.301 / 0.522); 200 items at 5%: 0.867 / 0.378 vs results 0.884 / 0.386 (difference about 0.017 in coverage, consistent with Monte Carlo error of about 0.005 to 0.01 per run; I did not pin it down). The README table, the 69-85% / 12-16% strata shares and the recall-estimate example (0.715 at 2% of 100 items, 0.365 at 50%) all agree with results.txt line by line. Caps at 3 because the split, truth and coders were all built from the same shared qual-real loader and the naive-Bayes coder was not independently reimplemented.
evidence.completeness: Claimed items checked: (a) 7 unit tests pass; (b) run.py reproduces results.txt exactly; (c) figure.py ran and rewrote width_by_share.svg with no tracked diff; (d) all 8 results sections are present and the README table is copied from sections 5 and 6; (e) the recall estimator exists and is reported (section 7); (f) the draw/dropped-draw count is reported (section 8, zero dropped, so no survivorship in the cells); (g) Next steps (real LLM coder, Wilson stratum interval, group gap and regression) are honestly marked not done. Not exercised: the live page https://marisstella.app/research/qual-lowrate/ was not loaded. Minor inconsistency: project.json says 2-20 audited negatives, the README says 2-10 for 2-5% of 100-200 items (both fit their own ranges). Dead code: sampling_rates() and weighted_prevalence() are never used by run.py.
evidence.verification: Test command: `cd research/qual-lowrate && python3 -m unittest test_qualrate`, 7 tests, OK, 0.09 s. Five hand-seeded mutations in qualrate.py, each reverted with `git checkout research/qual-lowrate/qualrate.py`. (1) draw(): `share_pos=1 - neg_share` -> `share_pos=neg_share` (swaps the strata): caught. (2) recall(): `fn = len(neg)*mean` -> `len(pos)*mean`: caught. (3) draw(): `neg_share <= 0` -> `< 0` (positives-only design no longer taken at share 0): caught. (4) recall(): denominator `tp+fn` -> `tp+fn+1e-3`: caught. (5) sampling_rates(): `n1 = ... n_gold - n0` -> `n_gold - n0 - 1`: NOT caught (7 OK), because the test only asserts the negative-stratum rate. So 4 of 5 caught. Weakness: the headline simulation (coverage, width, bias on real data) has no test; the tests are synthetic and check the draw sizes, weighted vs stratified equivalence, rough unbiasedness (delta 0.006), and that a lower share widens the SE. The estimator actually used for every reported number, qa.stratified, lives in qual-labelaudit and is not under this directory's tests. A mutation there was not run.
evidence.craft: Read qualrate.py (49 lines), experiments/run.py, test_qualrate.py, and qual-labelaudit/qualaudit.py (draw, stratified, allocation). Small, readable, seeded, stdlib only, with docstrings stating assumptions (assume_zero_negatives, FPC ignored). Defects: (1) the module is mostly a thin wrapper: weighted_prevalence and sampling_rates are not called by the experiment, so the code that produced the results is qa.stratified, and the 'inclusion-probability weights' module is a parallel restatement verified only against it; (2) draw() has a floor of two items per stratum (max(2, ...)), so a requested 2% of 100 items is exactly 2 and 2% of 200 is 4, which makes the 'share' axis partially a minimum-count axis, not stated in the README; (3) the sys.path.insert chain across four sibling projects (qual-labelaudit -> qual-gapaudit -> qual-correction, plus qual-real's run.py imported as `run`, which collides with this directory's own run.py name) is fragile; (4) run.py docstring says 'about a minute' while README says ~10 s (measured 8.7 s); (5) the same 1,000 draws use one shared RNG across cells so cells are not independent of order (fine but undocumented); (6) no handling of a design where a stratum has fewer than 2 items, it is silently skipped and counted, which is acceptable and reported.
evidence.claims: Checked each README claim against results.txt (and my recomputation): bias -0.117 to -0.160 with coverage 0.000 at share 0: yes; within +-0.012 at 2%, within +-0.008 from 5%: yes (largest are +0.0112 and +0.0060); widths 0.126 / 0.188 / 0.259 / 0.352 at 200 items: yes; worst coverage 0.85 at 5% and 0.51 at 2%, 0.26 at 100 items 2% and 0.58 at 5%: yes; Neyman share 0.63-0.82: yes; stratum 69-85% of corpus: yes; coverage 0.93+ from 30% at 100 items: 0.928 worst-coder, so 'or more' is a hair off (0.93 rounded); about 0.91 at 10% with 400: 0.911 yes. Runtime '~10 s': measured 8.7 s. The 'not LLMs' limitation is stated up top, in Limitations and in the title block; the produced-with-AI note is present; the recall limit (coders miss 47-65%, a high-recall coder untested) is stated and the result is explicitly not extended. The headline 'No' is scoped to these coders. One overreach: the lede says the optimum lies 'above half, the opposite direction to a low rate' using the oracle Neyman share, which is computed from the full evaluated data and for a Wald variance, a design-theory fact that needs no experiment (see fitness). No fabricated numbers found.
evidence.fitness: Research bar: a PhD-level programme aimed at a publishable result (research/CLAUDE.md, track qual). A practitioner designing a validation audit gets one usable rule (audit at least 20-40 coder-negatives, do not go to a low rate when the coder misses half) and a reproducible harness, but the result is a follow-up in a chain of small notes (qual-labelaudit, qual-correction, qual-negaudit) on one code, one corpus, one split, four weak coders and a Wald interval, with the decisive condition (high-recall LLM coder) not tested. Nearest prior work: Neyman (1934) and Cochran (1977) optimum allocation, which already says the allocation share is proportional to stratum size times within-stratum SD, so with a 12-16%-positive stratum making up 69-85% of the corpus the optimum necessarily puts most of the audit there; Horvitz-Thompson (1952); Angelopoulos et al. (2023) prediction-powered inference and its stratified/active variants (Zrnic and Candes 2024, active statistical inference, which samples where the model is uncertain); Egami et al. (2023) design-based supervised learning for LLM annotations, which also derives sampling by model confidence. Only Cochran, HT and PPI are cited; the active/confidence-sampling papers are not. The finding is sound but not new: it confirms a textbook allocation result on real data; the finite-sample under-coverage of Wald intervals at 2-10 audited items is also expected and reported. The new piece would be the high-recall LLM arm, which is not done.
evidence.domain: Compared with survey-sampling practice (Cochran ch. 5, 'optimum allocation'; two-phase / double sampling for misclassification, Tenenbein 1970). Matches: stratified mean with known stratum sizes, inclusion-probability weighting, Neyman allocation, coverage and width simulated against a truth that is the full-sample human mean, bias reported alongside. Departs: (1) the truth is the finite evaluated set's mean, the audit samples from that same set without replacement, but the SE drops the finite-population correction, so coverage is conservative at large n (README says so; it also means 'coverage 0.97' at 400 items is not a failure of calibration); (2) a statistician would use an interval that handles 2-10 items per stratum (Wilson/Agresti-Coull stratum intervals, a Bayesian beta-binomial, or the bootstrap) and would not call Wald results at 2 audited negatives a property of the design: the 'low rate breaks the interval' finding is largely a finding about the Wald method; (3) a variance with n_h=2 is itself estimated from two points, and a zero-variance stratum (all audited negatives human-negative) gives SE 0 for that stratum: this occurs often at 2-10 items with 12% prevalence and drives the coverage collapse, but the project does not decompose it; (4) a single code, corpus and train/test split, no repeats over splits, so the sampling variability of the coder itself is absent; (5) no cost model: an audit is judged by width at fixed n, not at fixed cost, and a practitioner choosing a lower rate has a reason in cost per item, which is not the same across strata; (6) no check against the closed-form expected variance, which would have replaced much of the simulation.

defects.what: The 'low rate breaks the interval' conclusion is confounded with the choice of a Wald interval at 2-10 audited items per stratum (and a two-item floor per stratum): zero-variance stratum draws give SE 0 and drive the collapse. The README does state Wald-only as a limitation, but the lede and summary present the under-coverage as a property of low-rate audits.

The central result (optimum allocation to the noisy stratum is above half, so a low rate widens the interval) follows from Neyman/Cochran allocation theory; the README cites Cochran but frames it as an empirical finding, and the nearest recent prior work on sampling by model confidence for LLM-annotation inference (Egami et al. 2023; Zrnic and Candes 2024) is not cited.

Test suite does not exercise the code that produced the results: weighted_prevalence and sampling_rates are not used by run.py, the estimator used is qa.stratified (another project), and the real-data simulation (coverage, width, bias) has no test. A seeded off-by-one in sampling_rates survived (1 of 5 mutations).

draw() enforces at least 2 audited items per stratum, so the 2% share at 100 items is a 2-item minimum rather than a rate; undocumented in the README, and 'share' and 'count' are conflated on the low end.
run.py docstring says 'about a minute', README says ~10 s (measured 8.7 s); project.json says 2-20 audited negatives, README 2-10.
Import of qual-real's run.py as `run` shadows this directory's own run.py name and relies on a four-project sys.path chain; coder is one split, no repeat over splits.

verdict: A tidy, honest, reproducible small study: run.py reproduces results.txt exactly in 9 s, my independent numpy implementation reproduced the lexicon coder's precision, recall, miss rate and Neyman share exactly and its coverage/width cells to within Monte Carlo error, and every checked README number agrees with results.txt. It meets the quality bar on the computed rule (correctness 3, claims 3, verification 2 is below 3, so it does NOT meet it: verification fails because the tests are synthetic, the headline estimator lives in another project, and 1 of 5 seeded mutations survived). The result is sound but not new: it confirms Neyman allocation and the known small-sample failure of Wald intervals on one corpus with weak, non-LLM coders, and the deciding experiment (a high-recall coder) is deferred. Cheap fixes: add a stratum interval that works at 2-10 items, cite the model-confidence-sampling literature, test the experiment path, and run the high-recall arm.
